Let's dive into Chapter 8: Workplaces That Inspire, Not Manipulate.
Think about your own job for a moment. Incentives are everywhere, right? There are bonuses for hitting your targets, awards for perfect attendance, and—of course—warnings if you miss a deadline.
The idea seems straightforward: reward the right behavior, punish the wrong, and everything should fall into place. But in reality, it doesn’t always work out that way.
What usually happens? Well, people start focusing on the numbers, not the mission. They do just enough to score the bonus, but rarely go above and beyond. Pretty soon, that sense of shared purpose fades away—replaced by competition and a bit of cynicism.
Some organizations get frustrated with this cycle, so they try a new approach. Instead of hanging carrots in front of employees or waving sticks, they build a culture around trust and shared goals.
For example, in one company, managers stopped giving out individual bonuses. Instead, they asked people what would actually make their work feel more meaningful. And the answers were eye-opening—employees wanted more of a voice in decisions, more chances to learn, and more time to work together as a team.
Now, this shift wasn’t easy. Some folks, who were used to competing for rewards, felt anxious about missing out. But as time passed, the culture changed. People began helping each other, sharing ideas, and taking real risks. Suddenly, the focus shifted from personal gain to collective success. The office started to feel less like a competition, and more like a true community.
In another example, a manager noticed her team was totally burned out from chasing targets. Instead of pushing them harder, she brought everyone together to talk about what truly mattered. Together, they set their own goals—based on what they cared about.
And the results? Not only did productivity go up, but morale soared. People felt genuine ownership over their work, and real pride in what they achieved.
What became clear was this: when employees feel trusted and included, they don’t need bribes or threats. They’re already motivated—driven by purpose and genuine connection. The manager’s job shifts, too—from being an enforcer or judge, to being a supporter and coach.
Most people don’t realize just how much the structure of work shapes motivation. If all you have are rewards and punishments, folks just learn how to play the game. But if you build trust, encourage collaboration, and focus on growth, people start to care about the work itself.
The real challenge isn’t just to take away incentives, but to build something better in their place. That means creating workplaces where people have real choices, where their voices truly matter, and where mistakes are seen as opportunities to learn.
It’s about trusting employees to care about their own work, and supporting them as they figure out what really matters to them.
